message.content:
The question asks whether two discrete random variables can have finite individual expectations while their sum has an undefined or infinite expectation.
The short answer is no under the standard definition of expectation for real valued random variables.
A finite expectation means that both the positive and negative parts of the variable are finite.
That condition is equivalent to the variable being integrable.
If a variable is integrable then its absolute value has a finite expectation.
For discrete random variables this follows from summing the absolute values against their probabilities.
The absolute value of a sum is bounded by the sum of the absolute values.
Therefore the expectation of the absolute value of the sum is bounded by the sum of the expectations.
Since both individual absolute expectations are finite the absolute expectation of the sum is finite.
A finite absolute expectation guarantees that the ordinary expectation exists and is finite.
Thus the sum cannot be undefined or infinite when the two inputs have finite expectations.
The same argument does not require independence.
It also does not require identical distributions.
It holds for any jointly distributed pair of integrable random variables.
The reason is that integrability is a stable property under addition.
If one tries to make the sum fail then one must lose integrability of at least one input.
A conditional or improper sum that looks finite is not enough if the positive or negative mass is infinite.
In probability finite expectation always controls both tails in the integrable sense.
This distinction matters when discussing conditionally convergent series.
A conditionally convergent series can assign a finite value in one order but not another.
The expectation of a random variable is not ordered arbitrarily over its values.
It is defined through positive and negative parts and this prevents that pathology for integrable variables.
Since finite expectations imply absolute integrability for every discrete variable the sum inherits absolute integrability and its expectation exists by linearity and no cancellation issue can ever make the combined expectation truly undefined beneath here.
